To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. subaqueous deposition of glacial sediments is a widespread phenomenon; 2. the chemical and physical properties of subaqueously-deposited glacial sediments differ from those of tills; 3. subaqueous-glaciation and post-glacial processes can account for the origin of many sedimentary rocks, such as siliceous shaly cherts and bedded barites.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the sedimentologic effects of glaciation on the oceans, and the effects of glaciation and post-glaciation on the chemistry of marine sediments.
the physical and chemical processes of sedimentation in intracontinental basins, with particular emphasis on the role of glaciation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

subaqueous-glaciation processes and the subsequent post-glacial history of a basin can be inferred from a knowledge of the physical and chemical characteristics and the depositional environments of glacial sediments.

subaqueous-glacigenic and post-glacial sediments in intra-continental basin are not uncommon and may have been deposited in a variety of environments and in association with a variety of depositional and diagenetic processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the glacial-marine environment is a dynamic one in which the sedimentary record of the environment is a reflection of the processes of sedimentation and diagenesis, rather than the processes that occurred before deposition.
glacial marine sedimentary rocks can be distinguished from tills and other glacial sediments by the presence of a marine fauna and by the chemical composition of the rock.

the glacial marine record in intra-continental settings is characterized by: 1. a high proportion of diamictites, 2. a low proportion of siliceous sediments, 3. an abundance of carbonates and barite, and 4. a low Fe content.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the physical and chemical characteristics (e.g., Fe content) of glaciomarine deposits can be explained by their mode of deposition.
subaqueous deposition and post-glacial processes may have been important contributors to the formation of many ancient diamictite and diamictite-associated deposits.
subaqueous glacial sedimentation and post-glacial chemical sedimentation in intracontinental basins can produce deposits that mimic those of the classic Phanerozoic epicontinental seas.
